after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}2 & a \\ 3 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{b}{a}.$
after.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Computing $A-3I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}]-(3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

content.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
content.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-1\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=3$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -6 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-3I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
content.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda  & 1 \\ -1 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (4-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-1\cdot (-1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=3.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-3I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

after.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
after.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

content.problem:
Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$, ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ are the respective eigenvectors. Find the matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=A,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.
content.worked_solution:
Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the eigenvalues of the matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3,$ we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ by writing the eigenvalues in the main diagonal:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$

Therefore, we get

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}].$
after.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}7-\lambda  & -6 \\ 8 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (7-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-(-6)\cdot 8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-49+48 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-1 & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 8 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}8 & -6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=4,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-1I & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 8 & -7\end{aligned}]-1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
